"""Minimal, dependency-free SVG charts for the strands-decider report.

Conventions (following the dataviz reference palette):
  * one y-axis per chart; separate measures get separate panels, never a second axis;
  * the default lineage (runs adopted as the default recipe) is series 1, a 2px line with
    8px dots; experiments that were not adopted are series 2, dots only, since they are
    branches, not steps along a line;
  * reference systems are hairline rules labelled at the right edge in muted ink;
  * text never wears a series colour; every mark carries a <title> for hover;
  * light and dark themes come from CSS custom properties and prefers-color-scheme.
Palette validated with the dataviz validator (both modes, all pairs): series 1/2 are
blue #2a78d6 / orange #eb6834 (dark #3987e5 / #d95926).
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
import math
from html import escape

FONT = 'system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", sans-serif'
STYLE = f"""<style>
.viz {{ --surface:#fcfcfb; --ink:#0b0b0b; --ink2:#52514e; --muted:#898781; --grid:#e1e0d9;
  --axis:#c3c2b7; --s1:#2a78d6; --s2:#eb6834; --s3:#1baf7a;
  --h0:#cde2fb; --h1:#9ec5f4; --h2:#6da7ec; --h3:#3987e5; --h4:#256abf; --h5:#184f95; --h6:#0d366b; }}
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {{
  .viz {{ --surface:#1a1a19; --ink:#ffffff; --ink2:#c3c2b7; --grid:#2c2c2a; --axis:#383835;
    --s1:#3987e5; --s2:#d95926; --s3:#199e70;
    --h0:#0d366b; --h1:#104281; --h2:#184f95; --h3:#1c5cab; --h4:#256abf; --h5:#3987e5; --h6:#6da7ec; }} }}
.viz text {{ font-family:{FONT}; fill:var(--ink2); font-size:11px; }}
.viz .title {{ fill:var(--ink); font-size:15px; font-weight:600; }}
.viz .subtitle {{ fill:var(--ink2); font-size:12px; }}
.viz .panel {{ fill:var(--ink); font-size:12px; font-weight:600; }}
.viz .muted {{ fill:var(--muted); }}
.viz .value {{ fill:var(--ink); font-weight:600; }}
.viz .tick {{ font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums; fill:var(--muted); }}
.viz .grid {{ stroke:var(--grid); stroke-width:1; }}
.viz .axis {{ stroke:var(--axis); stroke-width:1; }}
.viz .ref {{ stroke:var(--muted); stroke-width:1; }}
.viz .line1 {{ stroke:var(--s1); stroke-width:2; fill:none; stroke-linejoin:round; stroke-linecap:round; }}
.viz .line0, .viz .line2, .viz .line3 {{ stroke-width:1.5; fill:none; stroke-linejoin:round; stroke-linecap:round; }}
.viz .line0 {{ stroke:var(--ink2); }}
.viz .line2 {{ stroke:var(--s2); }}
.viz .line3 {{ stroke:var(--s3); }}
.viz .strip {{ fill:transparent; }}
.viz .strip:hover {{ fill:var(--grid); fill-opacity:0.5; }}
.viz .dot1 {{ fill:var(--s1); stroke:var(--surface); stroke-width:2; }}
.viz .dot2 {{ fill:var(--s2); stroke:var(--surface); stroke-width:2; }}
.viz .dot3 {{ fill:var(--s3); stroke:var(--surface); stroke-width:2; }}
.viz .dot1s {{ fill:var(--s1); fill-opacity:0.55; }}
.viz .arrow {{ fill:var(--s1); }}
.viz .hit {{ fill:transparent; }}
</style>"""


def _svg(width, height, body):
    return (f'<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" class="viz" width="{width}" height="{height}" '
            f'viewBox="0 0 {width} {height}" role="img">\n{STYLE}\n'
            f'<rect width="{width}" height="{height}" fill="var(--surface)"/>\n' + "\n".join(body) + "\n</svg>\n")


def text_width(s, size=11):
    return len(s) * size * 0.56


def nice_ticks(lo, hi, n=5):
    span = hi - lo
    raw = span / max(n, 1)
    mag = 10 ** math.floor(math.log10(raw))
    step = min((m * mag for m in (1, 2, 2.5, 5, 10) if m * mag >= raw), default=raw)
    start, end = math.floor(lo / step + 1e-9) * step, math.ceil(hi / step - 1e-9) * step
    ticks, t = [], start
    while t <= end + step * 1e-6:  # the range always covers the data: ends on a tick past hi
        ticks.append(round(t, 10))
        t += step
    return ticks, step


def _fmt(v, step):
    """Enough decimals to show the step exactly: a 0.025 step needs three, not two."""
    decimals = max(0, -math.floor(math.log10(step))) if step < 1 else 0
    while decimals < 6 and abs(round(step, decimals) - step) > 1e-9:
        decimals += 1
    return f"{v:.{decimals}f}"


def _title(s):
    return f"<title>{escape(s)}</title>"


def _plot(body, box, xs_labels, points, refs, ylabel=None, lower_is_better=False,
          label_last=True, y_range=None, cap=None):
    """Draw one dot/lineage panel into `body` inside box=(x, y, w, h).

    points: list of dicts {x_label, value, kind ('default'|'experiment'), tip}
    refs:   list of (label, value) horizontal reference rules
    """
    x0, y0, w, h = box
    vals = [p["value"] for p in points] + [v for _, v in refs]
    if y_range is not None:  # an explicit range is used as given
        ticks, step = nice_ticks(*y_range, 4)
    else:
        lo, hi = min(vals), max(vals)
        pad = (hi - lo) * 0.12 or 0.01
        ticks, step = nice_ticks(lo - pad, min(hi + pad, cap) if cap is not None else hi + pad, 4)
        if cap is not None:  # e.g. accuracy: no tick above 1.0
            ticks = [t for t in ticks if t <= cap + 1e-9]
            if ticks[-1] < hi:
                ticks.append(cap)
    ylo, yhi = ticks[0], ticks[-1]
    ref_space = max((text_width(lbl) for lbl, _ in refs), default=0) + (10 if refs else 0)
    pw = w - ref_space

    def ypos(v):
        return y0 + h - (v - ylo) / (yhi - ylo) * h

    band = pw / len(xs_labels)

    def xpos(lbl):
        return x0 + band * (xs_labels.index(lbl) + 0.5)

    for t in ticks:  # recessive hairline grid + tick labels
        y = ypos(t)
        body.append(f'<line class="grid" x1="{x0}" x2="{x0 + pw}" y1="{y:.1f}" y2="{y:.1f}"/>')
        body.append(f'<text class="tick" x="{x0 - 6}" y="{y + 3.5:.1f}" text-anchor="end">{_fmt(t, step)}</text>')
    body.append(f'<line class="axis" x1="{x0}" x2="{x0 + pw}" y1="{y0 + h}" y2="{y0 + h}"/>')
    for lbl in xs_labels:
        body.append(f'<text x="{xpos(lbl):.1f}" y="{y0 + h + 16}" text-anchor="middle">{escape(lbl)}</text>')
    note = ", ".join(x for x in (ylabel, "lower is better" if lower_is_better else None) if x)
    if note:  # above the plot, starting at the tick-label column so it is never clipped
        body.append(f'<text class="muted" x="{x0 - 40}" y="{y0 - 10}">{escape(note)}</text>')

    # reference systems, labelled at the right edge; labels closer than 12px are spread
    # apart so they never overprint (the rules themselves stay at their true values)
    placed = sorted(((ypos(v), lbl, v) for lbl, v in refs), key=lambda t: t[0])
    label_y = []
    for y, _, _ in placed:
        label_y.append(max(y, label_y[-1] + 12) if label_y else y)
    for (y, lbl, v), ly in zip(placed, label_y, strict=True):
        body.append(f'<g>{_title(f"{lbl}: {v:.3f}")}'
                    f'<line class="ref" x1="{x0}" x2="{x0 + pw}" y1="{y:.1f}" y2="{y:.1f}"/>'
                    f'<text class="muted" x="{x0 + pw + 6}" y="{ly + 3.5:.1f}">{escape(lbl)}</text></g>')

    lineage = [p for p in points if p["kind"] == "default"]
    if len(lineage) > 1:
        d = " ".join(f"{'M' if i == 0 else 'L'}{xpos(p['x_label']):.1f},{ypos(p['value']):.1f}"
                     for i, p in enumerate(lineage))
        body.append(f'<path class="line1" d="{d}"/>')
    for p in points:
        cx, cy = xpos(p["x_label"]), ypos(p["value"])
        cls = "dot1" if p["kind"] == "default" else "dot2"
        body.append(f'<g>{_title(p["tip"])}<circle class="hit" cx="{cx:.1f}" cy="{cy:.1f}" r="11"/>'
                    f'<circle class="{cls}" cx="{cx:.1f}" cy="{cy:.1f}" r="5"/></g>')
    if label_last and lineage:  # one direct label: where the lineage ends
        p = lineage[-1]
        label = p.get("label") or f"{p['value']:.3f}"
        body.append(f'<text class="value" x="{xpos(p["x_label"]):.1f}" y="{ypos(p["value"]) - 10:.1f}" '
                    f'text-anchor="middle">{escape(label)}</text>')


def _legend(body, x, y, with_experiments=True):
    body.append(f'<line class="line1" x1="{x}" x2="{x + 18}" y1="{y}" y2="{y}"/>'
                f'<circle class="dot1" cx="{x + 9}" cy="{y}" r="4"/>'
                f'<text x="{x + 24}" y="{y + 4}">adopted as the default recipe</text>')
    if with_experiments:
        x2 = x + 24 + text_width("adopted as the default recipe") + 24
        body.append(f'<circle class="dot2" cx="{x2 + 9}" cy="{y}" r="4"/>'
                    f'<text x="{x2 + 22}" y="{y + 4}">experiment, not adopted</text>')


def dot_chart(title, subtitle, xs_labels, points, refs=(), ylabel=None, lower_is_better=False,
              width=760, height=380, y_range=None, cap=None):
    body = [f'<text class="title" x="24" y="30">{escape(title)}</text>',
            f'<text class="subtitle" x="24" y="50">{escape(subtitle)}</text>']
    _legend(body, 24, 74, with_experiments=any(p["kind"] == "experiment" for p in points))
    _plot(body, (72, 118, width - 72 - 24, height - 118 - 44), xs_labels, points, list(refs),
          ylabel=ylabel, lower_is_better=lower_is_better, y_range=y_range, cap=cap)
    return _svg(width, height, body)


def small_multiples(title, subtitle, panels, xs_labels, width=760, panel_height=170, cols=1):
    """panels: list of dicts {title, points, refs, lower_is_better, ylabel}."""
    rows = math.ceil(len(panels) / cols)
    top = 100
    ph = panel_height
    height = top + rows * (ph + 70) + 10
    body = [f'<text class="title" x="24" y="30">{escape(title)}</text>',
            f'<text class="subtitle" x="24" y="50">{escape(subtitle)}</text>']
    _legend(body, 24, 74, with_experiments=any(p["kind"] == "experiment"
                                               for pan in panels for p in pan["points"]))
    colw = (width - 24) / cols
    for i, pan in enumerate(panels):
        r, c = divmod(i, cols)
        x = 24 + c * colw
        y = top + r * (ph + 70) + 30
        body.append(f'<text class="panel" x="{x}" y="{y - 8}">{escape(pan["title"])}</text>')
        _plot(body, (x + 48, y + 22, colw - 48 - 24, ph - 22), xs_labels, pan["points"],
              list(pan.get("refs", ())), ylabel=pan.get("ylabel"),
              lower_is_better=pan.get("lower_is_better", False), y_range=pan.get("y_range"),
              cap=pan.get("cap"))
    return _svg(width, height, body)


def heatmap(title, subtitle, row_labels, col_labels, cells, gap_before=None, width=None):
    """cells[(row, col)] = (value in [0, 1], tip). gap_before: col label to set apart."""
    cw, ch = 44, 26
    left = 24 + max(text_width(r, 11) for r in row_labels) + 12
    top = 96
    extra = 16 if gap_before else 0
    width = width or int(left + len(col_labels) * cw + extra + 24)
    height = top + len(row_labels) * ch + 90
    body = [f'<text class="title" x="24" y="30">{escape(title)}</text>',
            f'<text class="subtitle" x="24" y="50">{escape(subtitle)}</text>']

    def cx(j):
        return left + j * cw + (extra if gap_before and j >= col_labels.index(gap_before) else 0)

    for j, c in enumerate(col_labels):
        body.append(f'<text x="{cx(j) + cw / 2:.1f}" y="{top - 8}" text-anchor="middle">{escape(c)}</text>')
    for i, r in enumerate(row_labels):
        y = top + i * ch
        body.append(f'<text x="{left - 10}" y="{y + ch / 2 + 4:.1f}" text-anchor="end">{escape(r)}</text>')
        for j, c in enumerate(col_labels):
            if (r, c) not in cells:
                continue
            v, tip = cells[(r, c)]
            b = min(6, int(v * 7))  # seven sequential bins, 0-1
            body.append(f'<rect x="{cx(j) + 1:.1f}" y="{y + 1}" width="{cw - 2}" height="{ch - 2}" rx="3" '
                        f'fill="var(--h{b})">{_title(tip)}</rect>')
    # ramp legend
    ly = top + len(row_labels) * ch + 30
    body.append(f'<text x="{left}" y="{ly - 8}">accuracy</text>')
    for b in range(7):
        body.append(f'<rect x="{left + b * 34}" y="{ly}" width="32" height="12" rx="2" fill="var(--h{b})"/>')
        body.append(f'<text class="tick" x="{left + b * 34}" y="{ly + 26}">{b / 7:.2f}</text>')
    body.append(f'<text class="tick" x="{left + 7 * 34}" y="{ly + 26}">1.00</text>')
    return _svg(width, height, body)


def _scatter_panel(body, box, spec, points, lineage, x_range, y_range, arrow_id):
    """One accuracy-vs-error panel. points: dicts {id, x, y, kind, tip, label?, dx?, dy?}."""
    x0, y0, w, h = box
    xt, xs = nice_ticks(*x_range, 5)
    yt, ys = nice_ticks(*y_range, 4)

    def X(v):
        return x0 + (v - xt[0]) / (xt[-1] - xt[0]) * w

    def Y(v):
        return y0 + h - (v - yt[0]) / (yt[-1] - yt[0]) * h

    for t in yt:
        body.append(f'<line class="grid" x1="{x0}" x2="{x0 + w}" y1="{Y(t):.1f}" y2="{Y(t):.1f}"/>')
        body.append(f'<text class="tick" x="{x0 - 6}" y="{Y(t) + 3.5:.1f}" text-anchor="end">{_fmt(t, ys)}</text>')
    for t in xt:
        body.append(f'<line class="grid" x1="{X(t):.1f}" x2="{X(t):.1f}" y1="{y0}" y2="{y0 + h}"/>')
        body.append(f'<text class="tick" x="{X(t):.1f}" y="{y0 + h + 16}" text-anchor="middle">{_fmt(t, xs)}</text>')
    body.append(f'<line class="axis" x1="{x0}" x2="{x0 + w}" y1="{y0 + h}" y2="{y0 + h}"/>')
    body.append(f'<text class="panel" x="{x0 - 40}" y="{y0 - 14}">{escape(spec["title"])}</text>')
    xlabel = spec.get("xlabel", "JevBench accuracy")
    body.append(f'<text class="muted" x="{x0 + w}" y="{y0 + h + 34}" text-anchor="end">{escape(xlabel)} &#8594;</text>')
    better, corner = spec.get("better", ("better: right and down", "bottom"))
    by = y0 + h - 8 if corner == "bottom" else y0 + 14
    body.append(f'<text class="muted" x="{x0 + w - 4}" y="{by}" text-anchor="end">{escape(better)}</text>')

    by_id = {p["id"]: p for p in points}
    path = [by_id[i] for i in lineage if i in by_id]
    for a, b in itertools.pairwise(path):  # the lineage, one arrow per adoption
        body.append(f'<line class="line1" x1="{X(a["x"]):.1f}" y1="{Y(a["y"]):.1f}" x2="{X(b["x"]):.1f}" '
                    f'y2="{Y(b["y"]):.1f}" marker-end="url(#{arrow_id})"/>')
    order = {"experiment": 0, "reference": 1, "default": 2}  # lineage drawn on top
    for p in sorted(points, key=lambda p: order[p["kind"]]):
        cx, cy = X(p["x"]), Y(p["y"])
        if p["kind"] == "reference":  # squares: shape as well as colour
            mark = f'<rect class="dot3" x="{cx - 5:.1f}" y="{cy - 5:.1f}" width="10" height="10" rx="2"/>'
        else:
            mark = f'<circle class="{"dot1" if p["kind"] == "default" else "dot2"}" cx="{cx:.1f}" cy="{cy:.1f}" r="5"/>'
        body.append(f'<g>{_title(p["tip"])}<circle class="hit" cx="{cx:.1f}" cy="{cy:.1f}" r="11"/>{mark}</g>')
        if p.get("label"):
            dx, dy = p.get("dx", 8), p.get("dy", -8)
            anchor = "end" if dx < 0 else "middle" if dx == 0 else "start"
            if p.get("leader"):  # label set away from a crowded spot, joined by a hairline
                body.append(f'<line class="ref" x1="{cx:.1f}" y1="{cy - 6:.1f}" x2="{cx + dx:.1f}" y2="{cy + dy + 3:.1f}"/>')
            body.append(f'<text x="{cx + dx:.1f}" y="{cy + dy:.1f}" text-anchor="{anchor}">{escape(p["label"])}</text>')


def trajectory(title, subtitle, panels, lineage, note=None, width=980, panel_h=360,
               ref_label="other systems, same 231 tasks"):
    """Side-by-side accuracy-vs-error panels. panels: dicts {title, points, x_range, y_range}."""
    top = 104
    height = top + panel_h + 70 + (22 if note else 0)
    body = [f'<text class="title" x="24" y="30">{escape(title)}</text>',
            f'<text class="subtitle" x="24" y="50">{escape(subtitle)}</text>',
            '<defs><marker id="arr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" '
            'orient="auto-start-reverse"><path class="arrow" d="M0,1 L10,5 L0,9 z"/></marker></defs>']
    x = 24
    has_exp = any(p["kind"] == "experiment" for pan in panels for p in pan["points"])
    _legend(body, x, 74, with_experiments=has_exp)
    lx = x + 24 + text_width("adopted as the default recipe") + 24
    if has_exp:
        lx += 22 + text_width("experiment, not adopted") + 24
    body.append(f'<rect class="dot3" x="{lx + 4:.1f}" y="69" width="10" height="10" rx="2"/>'
                f'<text x="{lx + 20:.1f}" y="78">{escape(ref_label)}</text>')
    pw = (width - 2 * 24 - 64 * len(panels) - 24 * (len(panels) - 1)) / len(panels)
    for i, pan in enumerate(panels):
        bx = 24 + 64 + i * (pw + 64 + 24)
        _scatter_panel(body, (bx, top + 20, pw, panel_h - 20), pan, pan["points"], lineage,
                       pan["x_range"], pan["y_range"], "arr")
    if note:
        body.append(f'<text class="muted" x="24" y="{height - 14}">{escape(note)}</text>')
    return _svg(width, height, body)


def _numeric_axes(body, box, x_range, y_range, xlabel, ylabel, x_fmt, y_fmt, y_ticks, cap, x_ticks):
    """Grid, ticks and axis labels for a plot with numeric x; returns (X, Y, y formatter)."""
    x0, top, pw, plot_h = box
    yt, ys = nice_ticks(*y_range, y_ticks)
    if cap is not None:
        yt = [t for t in yt if t <= cap + 1e-9]
    xlo, xhi = x_range
    if x_ticks is None:
        x_ticks, _ = nice_ticks(xlo, xhi, 5)
    xt = [t for t in x_ticks if xlo - 1e-9 <= t <= xhi + 1e-9]

    def X(v):
        return x0 + (v - xlo) / (xhi - xlo) * pw

    def Y(v):
        return top + plot_h - (v - yt[0]) / (yt[-1] - yt[0]) * plot_h

    yf = y_fmt or (lambda v: _fmt(v, ys))
    for t in yt:
        body.append(f'<line class="grid" x1="{x0}" x2="{x0 + pw}" y1="{Y(t):.1f}" y2="{Y(t):.1f}"/>')
        body.append(f'<text class="tick" x="{x0 - 6}" y="{Y(t) + 3.5:.1f}" text-anchor="end">{yf(t)}</text>')
    body.append(f'<line class="axis" x1="{x0}" x2="{x0 + pw}" y1="{top + plot_h}" y2="{top + plot_h}"/>')
    for t in xt:
        body.append(f'<text class="tick" x="{X(t):.1f}" y="{top + plot_h + 16}" text-anchor="middle">{x_fmt.format(t)}</text>')
    body.append(f'<text class="muted" x="{x0 + pw}" y="{top + plot_h + 34}" text-anchor="end">{escape(xlabel)} &#8594;</text>')
    body.append(f'<text class="muted" x="{x0 - 40}" y="{top - 12}">{escape(ylabel)}</text>')
    return X, Y, yf


def line_chart(title, subtitle, series, xlabel, ylabel, x_range, y_range, notes=(), width=760,
               plot_h=300, cap=None, markers=False, x_fmt="{:,.0f}", y_fmt=None, y_ticks=4,
               x_ticks=None, x_name="step"):
    """Lines over a numeric x axis (e.g. training step).

    series: dicts {label, end_label, cls ('0'-'3'), points [(x, y)]}. Two or more series get a
    legend and a direct label at each line's end; one series gets neither (the title names
    it). A hover strip per x value lists every series' value there, a static stand-in for a
    crosshair; with markers, each point is also a dot with its own tooltip. x_ticks fixes the
    x tick positions; x_name is what the tooltips call x.
    """
    multi = len(series) > 1
    top = 116 if multi else 84
    x0 = 72
    end_space = max((text_width(s["end_label"]) for s in series), default=0) + 20 if multi else 24
    pw = width - x0 - end_space
    height = top + plot_h + 44 + 18 * len(notes) + 10
    body = [f'<text class="title" x="24" y="30">{escape(title)}</text>',
            f'<text class="subtitle" x="24" y="50">{escape(subtitle)}</text>']
    if multi:  # legend, in series order
        lx = 24
        for s in series:
            body.append(f'<line class="line{s["cls"]}" x1="{lx}" x2="{lx + 18}" y1="74" y2="74"/>'
                        f'<text x="{lx + 24}" y="78">{escape(s["label"])}</text>')
            lx += 24 + text_width(s["label"]) + 22
    X, Y, yf = _numeric_axes(body, (x0, top, pw, plot_h), x_range, y_range, xlabel, ylabel,
                             x_fmt, y_fmt, y_ticks, cap, x_ticks)

    # hover strips, drawn under the lines
    xs = sorted({x for s in series for x, _ in s["points"]})
    at = [{x: y for x, y in s["points"]} for s in series]
    for i, x in enumerate(xs):
        left = X((xs[i - 1] + x) / 2) if i else X(x) - 4
        right = X((x + xs[i + 1]) / 2) if i + 1 < len(xs) else X(x) + 4
        vals = "; ".join(f"{s['label']} {yf(a[x]) if y_fmt else f'{a[x]:.3f}'}"
                         for s, a in zip(series, at, strict=True) if x in a)
        body.append(f'<rect class="strip" x="{left:.1f}" y="{top}" width="{right - left:.1f}" height="{plot_h}">'
                    f'{_title(f"{x_name} {x_fmt.format(x)}: {vals}")}</rect>')

    for s in reversed(series):  # the first series is drawn last, on top
        d = " ".join(f"{'M' if i == 0 else 'L'}{X(x):.1f},{Y(y):.1f}" for i, (x, y) in enumerate(s["points"]))
        body.append(f'<path class="line{s["cls"]}" d="{d}" pointer-events="none"/>')
        if markers:
            for x, y in s["points"]:
                tip = f"{x_name} {x_fmt.format(x)}: {s['label']} {yf(y) if y_fmt else f'{y:.3f}'}"
                body.append(f'<g>{_title(tip)}<circle class="hit" cx="{X(x):.1f}" cy="{Y(y):.1f}" r="11"/>'
                            f'<circle class="dot{s["cls"]}" cx="{X(x):.1f}" cy="{Y(y):.1f}" r="4"/></g>')

    if multi:  # direct labels at each line's end, spread to a 12px minimum gap
        ends = sorted(((Y(s["points"][-1][1]), s) for s in series), key=lambda t: t[0])
        placed = []
        for y, _ in ends:
            placed.append(max(y, placed[-1] + 12) if placed else y)
        for (_, s), ly in zip(ends, placed, strict=True):
            body.append(f'<text x="{X(s["points"][-1][0]) + 6:.1f}" y="{ly + 3.5:.1f}">{escape(s["end_label"])}</text>')
    elif series:  # one series: label its last value
        x, y = series[0]["points"][-1]
        body.append(f'<text class="value" x="{X(x):.1f}" y="{Y(y) - 10:.1f}" text-anchor="end">'
                    f'{yf(y) if y_fmt else f"{y:.3f}"}</text>')
    for i, n in enumerate(notes):
        body.append(f'<text class="muted" x="24" y="{top + plot_h + 60 + 18 * i}">{escape(n)}</text>')
    return _svg(width, height, body)


def scatter_chart(title, subtitle, points, xlabel, ylabel, x_range, y_range, refs=(), notes=(),
                  width=760, plot_h=300, x_fmt="{:,.0f}", y_fmt=None, y_ticks=4, x_ticks=None):
    """One series of points over numeric axes, with optional horizontal reference rules.

    points: dicts {x, y, tip}. refs: (label, value) rules, labelled at the right edge and
    spread to a 12px minimum gap, as in the dot charts. Dots are translucent so dense
    regions read darker; each carries its own tooltip.
    """
    top, x0 = 84, 72
    ref_space = max((text_width(lbl) for lbl, _ in refs), default=0) + (16 if refs else 0)
    pw = width - x0 - 24 - ref_space
    height = top + plot_h + 44 + 18 * len(notes) + 10
    body = [f'<text class="title" x="24" y="30">{escape(title)}</text>',
            f'<text class="subtitle" x="24" y="50">{escape(subtitle)}</text>']
    X, Y, yf = _numeric_axes(body, (x0, top, pw, plot_h), x_range, y_range, xlabel, ylabel,
                             x_fmt, y_fmt, y_ticks, None, x_ticks)
    for p in points:
        body.append(f'<g>{_title(p["tip"])}<circle class="hit" cx="{X(p["x"]):.1f}" cy="{Y(p["y"]):.1f}" r="6"/>'
                    f'<circle class="dot1s" cx="{X(p["x"]):.1f}" cy="{Y(p["y"]):.1f}" r="3.5"/></g>')
    placed = sorted(((Y(v), lbl, v) for lbl, v in refs), key=lambda t: t[0])
    label_y = []
    for y, _, _ in placed:
        label_y.append(max(y, label_y[-1] + 12) if label_y else y)
    for (y, lbl, v), ly in zip(placed, label_y, strict=True):
        body.append(f'<g>{_title(f"{lbl}: {yf(v)}")}'
                    f'<line class="ref" x1="{x0}" x2="{x0 + pw}" y1="{y:.1f}" y2="{y:.1f}" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/>'
                    f'<text x="{x0 + pw + 6}" y="{ly + 3.5:.1f}">{escape(lbl)}</text></g>')
    for i, n in enumerate(notes):
        body.append(f'<text class="muted" x="24" y="{top + plot_h + 60 + 18 * i}">{escape(n)}</text>')
    return _svg(width, height, body)

---
name: customize-decider
description: >
  Guide a user from "I have a decision in my application" to a Strands Decider model that is
  measured on their own data, and trained only if the measurement says so. Use when a user
  wants to evaluate Strands Decider on their use case, compare the released models, decide
  whether to train a customized model, build a training set from their data, run and monitor
  the training, calibrate it, or ship and check it. Also use when a user asks "will the decider
  work for my task", "how do I train the decider on my data", "which size should I use", or
  "is my trained model better".
---

# Customize Strands Decider for a user's decisions

The purpose: help a user find out, with numbers from their own data, whether a released decider
already does their job, and if not, train one that does. Measure first. Train only when the
measurement shows a gap that training can close.

You are the user's guide. The user owns two kinds of decisions; ask before each one:

- **Money:** every GPU host, its shape, region and hours.
- **Data:** anything that moves their data off their machine (a cloud host, an LLM API used for
  labelling, an S3 bucket), and who may label it.

The reference files in `references/` hold the detail; read each one when its phase starts.

| phase | what you produce | gate to pass before the next phase |
|---|---|---|
| Setup | a repository checkout and a work directory | `strands-decider --help` runs from the checkout |
| 0. Fit | one paragraph: is a decider the right tool | the decision has a fixed set of options |
| 1. Task card | `work/task-card.md` | the user agrees with every question and option text |
| 2. Evaluation set | `work/eval/` frozen with hashes | enough items, labels audited, every row passes the row check |
| 3. Baselines | `work/baselines.md` | every candidate size and the user's current method scored on the same items |
| 4. Decision | `work/decision.md` | the user picks the customization tier |
| 5. Training data | `work/train/` frozen with hashes | row check passes, overlap with the evaluation set is zero |
| 6. Training | checkpoints of 3 seeds | smoke run passes, loss curves healthy |
| 7. Soup, calibrate, compare | `work/results.md` | the new model beats the baseline by more than the noise |
| 8. Ship and watch | serving command, thresholds, a re-check plan | the user accepts the thresholds |

Write a short dated log as you go (`work/LOG.md`): the exact command, what you saw, with numbers
and paths, and what you concluded.

## Setup

The skill needs the repository, not only the PyPI package: the PyPI package serves models only.
Training, evaluation, calibration, soups and the corpus tools are modules under `training/`, run as
`python -m training.<module>` from the checkout root.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/strands-labs/strands-decider && cd strands-decider
python3 -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e ".[train,dev]"        # serving only: pip install -e .
```

Paths in this skill are relative to the root of that checkout, and every command runs from there;
run the scripts in `work/` with `PYTHONPATH=.` so that they can import `training`. Create the work directory outside
the checkout (for example `../decider-work`, called `work/` below) and keep it out of git: it
holds the user's data. Run commands from the checkout root, with `work/` pointing there
(`ln -s ../decider-work work` is the simplest way).

## Phase 0. Is a decider the right tool?

A decider reads a state (text, structured data, or an image for the Qwen3.5 model) and a question,
and returns a probability distribution over options in one forward pass. It does not generate
text. Three question types:

- `noul`: yes/no, returns P(yes).
- `choice`: one of N named options (2 to 255), returns the pick, every option's probability and a
  confidence.
- `score`: an ordered rubric of 2 to 10 levels, returns the expected level and a confidence.

Good fits: routing, triage, tool selection, guardrails and policy checks, answer-adequacy checks,
grading against a rubric. The application can act on confident answers and send the rest to an
LLM or a person.

Poor fits: the answer is free text; the options are not known before the call; the decision needs
many steps of reasoning that are not in the state; the state is much longer than the serving
window (4,096 tokens by default; see `docs/inference.md`).

If it is a poor fit, say so and stop.

## Phase 1. The task card

Interview the user, then write `work/task-card.md`. One section per decision:

- The decision in one sentence, and what the application does with each answer.
- The question type, the exact instruction text, and the options. For `choice`, give each option
  a one-line description; for `noul`, describe what "true" and "false" mean. The model reads the
  descriptions.
- What the state contains, and an example state.
- The cost of each kind of error (for example, a false "urgent" wakes a person at night, a missed
  "urgent" loses a customer). This sets the thresholds in Phase 8.
- Where the labels come from (next section).

**Where labels come from.** Look for an outcome the user already records:

- A final outcome is a better label than a first guess. For example, if tickets record the team
  that finally closed them and whether they were reassigned, the final team is the label, and the
  reassignment rate of the current process is a free baseline (its accuracy is about
  1 âˆ’ reassignment rate). Keep the reassigned items as their own `task` in the evaluation set: they
  are the hard cases.
- If no field holds the label (for example "is this urgent?" when nobody recorded urgency), the
  label must be made. Plan it with the user: how many items (Phase 2 sizes), who labels them, and a
  one-page label guide with examples. A released decider's answers can pre-label the items for
  people to correct, which is fast; keep a few hundred items labelled blind to measure how much the
  pre-labels bias the people. An external LLM as a labeller sends the data off the machine: ask.

Try the questions on real examples with a released model before you build anything. `ask`
does not send option descriptions (`--choice` sets every description to empty, and option names
cannot contain commas), so test through the server, which takes the full request:

```bash
strands-decider serve StrandsAgents/strands-decider-E4B-gemma4-v1-2610 --port 8000 &
curl -s localhost:8000/v1/systemone -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{
  "state": "Help! My payouts have been failing for 3 days!",
  "questions": {
    "team": {"type": "choice", "instructions": "Which team should handle this ticket?",
             "criteria": {"billing": "payments, payouts, invoices", "sales": "pricing, new accounts"}},
    "urgent": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Does the customer need help today?",
               "criteria": {"true": "money is blocked or the service is down", "false": "it can wait"}}}}'
```

Revise the wording with the user on 20 to 50 real examples. Rewording the instructions and the
descriptions is free and often moves accuracy by several points.

## Phase 2. The evaluation set, before any training

Read `references/evaluation.md` and `references/data-format.md`. In short:

- Build the evaluation set from the user's real data, in the row format of `data-format.md`.
  Audit the labels with a second labeller.
- Size: at least 1,000 test items per decision, plus about as many for calibration. `eval` and
  `calibrate` split one file into two disjoint halves of about equal size.
- Split rule (one rule, applied in this order):
  1. Time cutoff: the most recent period is the evaluation set, the older data is for training.
  2. Then drop from the training side every group (customer, document, conversation) that also
     appears in the evaluation set.
  3. All rows of one state (several questions about one ticket) stay on the same side.
- Run the row check of `data-format.md` on the file. It catches rows that would stop `eval` or
  training (bad option names, too few options, a state longer than the window).
- Freeze it: write `work/eval/SHA256SUMS` and do not change the files afterwards. A changed
  evaluation set makes every earlier number incomparable.

## Phase 3. Baselines

Candidates: every released model the user can serve (2B Qwen3.5; Gemma 4 E2B, E4B, 12B, 26B-A4B;
README "Gemma 4 models" gives memory and latency), and the user's current method.

On an NVIDIA GPU, score with the CLI. Pass `--limit` above the file size (the default is 4,000):

```bash
python -m training.evaluate eval StrandsAgents/strands-decider-E4B-gemma4-v1-2610 \
  --data work/eval/eval.jsonl --limit 1000000 --out work/baselines/e4b.json
```

`eval` and `calibrate` take `--device cuda|mps|cpu` (default: the best available), and run the
model as `serve` does on that device. For per-item results (the paired comparison of Phase 7), use
the script in `references/evaluation.md`.

`eval` prints accuracy, ECE and NLL, by kind, by task and by confidence band. Score the user's
current method on the same test-half rows with their own code, and record its latency and cost.

Then recalibrate the best candidates on the user's data. This needs no training and is often the
largest cheap gain in calibration. `calibrate` writes into the checkpoint and refuses a Hub id, so
download a local copy first:

```bash
hf download StrandsAgents/strands-decider-E4B-gemma4-v1-2610 --local-dir work/models/e4b
python -m training.evaluate calibrate work/models/e4b --data work/eval/eval.jsonl --limit 1000000
python -m training.evaluate eval work/models/e4b --data work/eval/eval.jsonl --limit 1000000 --out work/baselines/e4b-cal.json
```

It fits on the `calib` half; `eval` scores the `test` half.

Write `work/baselines.md`: one row per candidate, with accuracy (and its 95% interval), ECE, the
share of answers at confidence â‰¥ 0.9 and their accuracy, latency, and memory. The first row is
always the majority-class baseline: per decision, the share of the test half whose label is the
most common label. It costs nothing to compute. A model below it has learned nothing useful for
that decision, however high its accuracy looks: 29% on a 10-way choice is below a 30% majority
class.

## Phase 4. Decide the customization tier

Read the table with the user. Climb this ladder and stop at the first rung that meets the user's
target:

1. **Reword** the instructions and descriptions (Phase 1). Re-score.
2. **Recalibrate** a released model on the user's data (Phase 3).
3. **Choose a larger released size.** A larger base model usually gains more than training a
   small one, and needs no training data.
4. **Fine-tune the released model** of the chosen size on the user's rows plus the public corpus
   (`init_from`, Phases 5 and 6). It must beat the released model on the user's test half to be
   worth serving.

Tier 4 is worth it when all of these hold: the gap to the target is larger than the noise of the
evaluation set (Phase 2 interval); the user can produce enough correct training labels (a few
thousand rows per decision is a sensible start, and gains usually flatten in the tens of
thousands); and the user accepts the cost of a GPU host (`references/training.md`). Fine-tune
the released model of the size the user will serve. Smaller models gain more from training than
larger ones.

Write `work/decision.md`: the tier, the reason in numbers, the target to beat, and the cost. The
user decides.

## Phase 5. Build the training data (tier 4)

Read `references/data-format.md`.

- Convert the user's labelled examples to rows, from the training side of the Phase 2 split only.
- Check the overlap with the evaluation set (`data-format.md`): no shared group, no duplicate or
  near-duplicate state. Report the counts; both must be zero.
- Do not reweight labels by default: weights shift the model's priors, and calibration cannot
  undo a shifted prior. Reweight only if the minority labels fail in Phase 7, and re-check
  calibration after.
- Give each question two to four `instruction_variants`, so the model learns the task, not one
  phrasing.
- Add the public corpus (`references/training.md`, "Build the public corpus"). It keeps the model's
  general skills and its calibration on unfamiliar inputs.
- Run the row check, then `python -m training.data stats work/train/train.jsonl` and
  `python -m training.data peek work/train/train.jsonl --n 10`, and show the user what the model will
  see.
- Freeze `work/train/` with `SHA256SUMS`.

## Phase 6. Train

Read `references/training.md` and `training/AGENTS.md` (host rules: spend is the user's decision;
one name tag per agent; tear down every host).

1. Choose the host for the size (`training.md`, "Hosts"). Ask the user, with the price.
2. Copy the frozen data to the host (`training.md`, "Data to the host"). Ask the user first.
3. Write the config from the template. Smoke run: 20 steps; check the lines listed in
   `training.md`.
4. Train three seeds. One seed is not a result: the seed-to-seed standard deviation of one recipe
   is about 3 items of a 231-item benchmark.
5. Monitor while it trains (`training.md`, "Monitoring"). Stop a diverged run; do not average it
   into a soup.

## Phase 7. Soup, calibrate, compare

```bash
python -m training.soup work/ckpt/s0 work/ckpt/s1 work/ckpt/s2 --out work/ckpt/soup
python -m training.evaluate calibrate work/ckpt/soup --data work/eval/eval.jsonl --limit 1000000
python -m training.evaluate eval work/ckpt/soup --data work/eval/eval.jsonl --limit 1000000 --out work/results/soup.json
```

Compare the soup with the best Phase 3 candidate on the same test-half rows: the accuracy
difference with McNemar's test on per-item results (`evaluation.md`), ECE, and accuracy at the
Phase 8 thresholds. Check also that the model did not lose what the user still needs (a
general-skills set, or the evaluations in `evaluation/README.md`). Write `work/results.md`. If the
gain is inside the noise, say so: the training did not help, and the released model stays.

## Phase 8. Ship and watch

- Serve: `strands-decider serve <checkpoint> --port 8000` (`docs/inference.md` for devices,
  batching and the window). Always serve a calibrated checkpoint.
- Thresholds for `choice` and `score`: from the test-half `by_confidence_band` table and the error
  costs in the task card, choose the confidence at which the application acts without a check. The
  documented default bands (act at â‰¥ 0.9, confirm from 0.5 to 0.9, send to a person below 0.5) are
  a start, not a rule.
- Thresholds for `noul`: the answer is P(yes), with no separate confidence. Choose one or two cut
  points on P(yes) from the error costs: for example, page a person above 0.8, queue for review
  between 0.4 and 0.8, ignore below 0.4. Measure the hit rate and false-alarm rate of each cut on the
  test half.
- Watch: log every answer with its probabilities. Each month, or after a change in the traffic,
  label a fresh sample and re-run Phase 3 on it. A fall in accuracy at the same confidence means the
  traffic moved; recalibrate or retrain.

## Rules

- Measure before you train, and compare on the same frozen items every time.
- Never train on evaluation data, and never edit the evaluation set after Phase 2.
- Report intervals, not single numbers. State when a difference is inside the noise.
- Ask before every action that costs money or moves the user's data off their machine.
- Do not claim a gain that the paired comparison does not show.

# Row format for evaluation and training data

One row is one (state, question, answer) triple, one JSON object per line. Evaluation and
training files use the same format. The code is `training/data/format.py`
(`Example`).

## Fields

| field | required | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `kind` | yes | `"noul"`, `"choice"` or `"score"` |
| `state` | yes | the content to decide on: a string, or JSON data (rendered deterministically); may be `""` when the question carries the whole task |
| `instructions` | yes | the question text |
| `options` | yes | list of `[name, description]` pairs, in canonical order (see below) |
| `label` | yes | the index of the correct option in `options` |
| `task` | no | a name for the decision; `eval` reports accuracy per task |
| `weight` | no | loss weight of the row (default 1.0) |
| `instruction_variants` | no | other phrasings of the same question; training samples one per epoch |

Canonical order per kind:

- `noul`: exactly two options named `"false"` (first) and `"true"` (second). Label 0 is no, 1 is
  yes. Other names fail.
- `choice`: 2 to 255 options, any order; training shuffles the options at every epoch.
- `score`: 2 to 10 levels, ascending, lowest level first. The label is the level index; the model
  reads the descriptions as the level texts.

## Examples

```json
{"kind": "noul", "state": "Help! My payouts have been failing for 3 days!", "instructions": "Does this convey urgency?", "options": [["false", "no urgency"], ["true", "the writer needs help soon"]], "label": 1, "task": "urgency", "instruction_variants": ["Is the writer asking for fast help?"]}
{"kind": "choice", "state": "Help! My payouts have been failing for 3 days!", "instructions": "Which team should handle this?", "options": [["billing", "payments, payouts, invoices"], ["sales", "pricing and new accounts"], ["retail", "store operations"]], "label": 0, "task": "triage"}
{"kind": "score", "state": "Help! My payouts have been failing for 3 days!", "instructions": "How frustrated is the writer?", "options": [["0", "calm"], ["1", "frustrated"], ["2", "very frustrated"]], "label": 1, "task": "frustration"}
```

Use the same instruction and option text as the application will send at serving time. The server
builds the same prompt from a request (`src/strands_decider/schema.py`), so a mismatch between
training text and serving text is a distribution shift.

## Converting user data

- One labelled decision becomes one row. Several questions about one state become several rows
  with the same `state`; they stay on the same side of every split.
- Keep the split keys in a side file, not in the row: `work/<set>/keys.jsonl`, one line per row with
  the row index, the group id (customer, document, conversation) and the timestamp.
- Use the same option set for one decision in every row, in the same canonical order.
- Many options: keep the training config's `num_slots` at least the largest option count, or
  subsample options per row and always keep the gold one (`python -m training.data build
  --max-options` does this for the public corpus).

## The row check (run on every file before it is frozen)

`python -m training.data stats` checks `kind` and the label range only. The checks below otherwise
fail late, in the middle of `eval` or training: option names and counts are validated when the
question is built, and a prompt longer than the window stops the collator ("option span has no
tokens left"). Save as `work/check_rows.py` and run it from the checkout root with `PYTHONPATH=.`:

```python
"""python work/check_rows.py FILE BASE_MODEL [MAX_TOKENS]: fail on any row that would fail later."""
import sys
from collections import Counter

from transformers import AutoTokenizer

from training.data.format import read_jsonl
from strands_decider.prompting import build_prompt

path, base = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
max_tokens = int(sys.argv[3]) if len(sys.argv) > 3 else 4096
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(base)  # the base model of the checkpoint you will use
bad, long_rows = Counter(), []
for i, ex in enumerate(read_jsonl(path)):
    try:
        prompt, _ = build_prompt(ex.state, ex.to_question())
    except Exception as e:  # option names, option counts, level counts
        bad[f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}"[:120]] += 1
        continue
    n = len(tok(prompt)["input_ids"]) + 1  # +1 for a BOS token
    if n > max_tokens:
        long_rows.append((i, n))
print(f"invalid rows: {sum(bad.values())}")
for msg, c in bad.most_common(10):
    print(f"  {c} x {msg}")
print(f"rows over {max_tokens} tokens: {len(long_rows)} (first: {long_rows[:5]})")
sys.exit(1 if bad or long_rows else 0)
```

`read_jsonl` itself stops at the first row with an unknown `kind` or a label out of range; fix
that row and run the check again. Remove rows over the window from the file; do not truncate their
state, because a truncated state can remove the evidence for the label. Base models of the released
deciders: `Qwen/Qwen3.5-2B-Base` and `google/gemma-4-<size>-it`.

## Label quality

Labels set the ceiling. Before you trust an evaluation set:

1. Draw 200 rows at random. Have a second person label them without seeing the first label.
2. Report the agreement. Inspect every disagreement with the user and fix the label guide.
3. If agreement is below about 90%, fix the guide and relabel before you measure models: a model
   cannot be measured more precisely than its labels.

## Overlap check between training and evaluation

Run all three and report the counts; all must be zero before training.

1. Groups: no group id in both `work/train/` and `work/eval/` (from the `keys.jsonl` side files).
2. Exact duplicates: normalize each state (lowercase, collapse white space, strip punctuation) and
   hash it; no hash in both sets. This catches short states that the next check cannot.
3. Near-duplicates: split each normalized state into words and take every 13-word sequence. Flag a
   training row when it shares at least 20% of its 13-word sequences (or at least 10 of them) with
   any evaluation row.

Drop flagged training rows; never drop evaluation rows to fix an overlap. A short
standard-library script does all three; write it in `work/` and keep it with the log.

## Freezing a set

```bash
(cd work/eval && shasum -a 256 *.jsonl > SHA256SUMS)
```

Record the hash in `work/LOG.md`. Before each later measurement, run
`(cd work/eval && shasum -a 256 -c SHA256SUMS)`.

# Evaluation: design, size and comparison

## What to measure

- **Accuracy** on the test half, per decision (`task`) and overall.
- **Calibration**: expected calibration error (ECE), and the accuracy of the answers at
  confidence â‰¥ 0.9. The application uses the confidence to decide when to act alone, so a
  confident wrong answer is the failure that matters.
- **Coverage at a threshold**: the share of answers at or above the chosen confidence.
- **Latency and memory** on the hardware the user will serve on.

`python -m training.evaluate eval` prints accuracy, ECE, NLL and score MAE, by kind, by task and by
confidence band, and `--out` writes the full report as JSON.

## The two halves

`calibrate` and `eval` split one file by a hash of the row position into two halves of about
equal size (`--split calib` and
`--split test`, the defaults of each command). They never overlap, so calibration is fitted on
rows that the reported numbers do not use. Pass the same file to both. The split is by row, not by
group: that is correct for calibration, but the train/evaluation split must be by group (see
`data-format.md`).

Pass `--limit` above the file size: the default limit is 4,000 rows.

## How many items

The 95% interval of an accuracy p on n items is about Â±1.96Â·âˆš(p(1âˆ’p)/n):

| test items | interval at 80% accuracy |
|---|---|
| 200 | Â±5.5 points |
| 500 | Â±3.5 points |
| 1,000 | Â±2.5 points |
| 4,000 | Â±1.2 points |

Two models scored on the same items are compared with a paired test, which resolves smaller
differences than these intervals, but the table shows the scale. Ask for at least 1,000 test
items per decision when the user cares about differences of a few points, plus the same number
for calibration.

## Coverage of the real traffic

Sample the evaluation set the way the traffic arrives, not the way it is easy to collect:

- Keep the real label balance in the test set (balance the training set instead, with `weight`).
- Include the hard and rare cases on purpose, as a separate `task` name, so their accuracy is
  reported separately and does not hide in the average.
- For production logs, use the most recent period as the evaluation set.

## Comparing two models

Score both on the same frozen test half. Then:

1. Accuracy difference with McNemar's test on the paired per-item results. The `--out` report
   holds aggregates only, so get per-item results with the script below, once per model.
2. ECE of both, and accuracy at confidence â‰¥ 0.9 for both.
3. For trained models: three seeds or their soup, never the best single seed. The best of several
   seeds is a lucky draw.

A difference inside the noise is "no difference". Report it as such.

## Per-item scoring

`eval` writes aggregates only. For the paired test, score each model through the Python API. Save
as `work/score.py` and run it from the checkout root with `PYTHONPATH=.`:

```python
"""Per-item results of one model on the test half: python work/score.py MODEL DATA OUT [DEVICE]."""
import json
import sys

from training.data.format import read_jsonl
from training.evaluate import collect_logits, partition_examples, predictions_from_logits, summarise
from strands_decider.modeling import StrandsDeciderModel

model_path, data, out = sys.argv[1:4]
device = sys.argv[4] if len(sys.argv) > 4 else "cuda"  # or "mps", "cpu"
examples = partition_examples(list(read_jsonl(data)), "test")
model = StrandsDeciderModel.load(model_path)
logits, labels, slots, exs = collect_logits(model, examples, device=device, max_length=model.config.max_length)
t = getattr(model.config, "temperature_by_kind", None) or model.config.temperature  # as `eval` applies it
preds = predictions_from_logits(logits, labels, slots, exs, temperature=t,
                                ordinal_smoothing=model.config.ordinal_smoothing)
print(json.dumps(summarise(preds)["overall"]))
with open(out, "w") as fh:
    for p in preds:
        fh.write(json.dumps({"task": p.task, "kind": p.kind, "label": p.label, "pred": p.pred,
                             "correct": p.correct, "confidence": p.confidence, "probs": p.probs}) + "\n")
```

The script prepares the model as `serve` does on the device, like `eval`.

Rows come out in the order of the test half, so two output files pair line by line. McNemar's
test on the two `correct` columns: b = rows only model A gets right, c = rows only model B gets
right; with b + c â‰¥ 25, the statistic (|b âˆ’ c| âˆ’ 1)Â² / (b + c) above 3.84 means p < 0.05.

## Comparing with an LLM baseline

Run the user's current LLM prompt over the same test rows with the same instruction and option
text. Record accuracy, latency per decision and cost per 1,000 decisions. LLMs do not return a
calibrated confidence; if the user's method has a score, compare its accuracy at matched coverage.

# Training a customized decider

Read `training/README.md` (setup, Gemma 4 settings, several GPUs) and `training/AGENTS.md`
(host runbooks and ground rules) before the first run. This file says what to change for a
user's own decisions.

## What to train

Fine-tune the released decider of the size the user will serve: `init_from` starts from a trained
checkpoint (a Hub id or a local directory) and trains its LoRA adapter and its head on the user's
rows. `training/README.md`, "Fine-tuning a released model with `init_from`", has the details. The
points that matter here:

- The checkpoint fixes the architecture. Leave `base_model`, `num_slots`, `head_type`,
  `pointer_dim`, `head_hidden`, `use_lora`, `lora_r`, `lora_alpha`, `lora_targets` and `force_bos`
  out of the config: a config that sets one of them stops before the model loads, even at a value
  that looks harmless. Do not start from a copy of `configs/train.yaml`.
- Released models are soups, so the adapter has rank 48 (three seeds of rank 16). A soup of three
  fine-tunes of it has rank 144.
- Temperatures reset to 1: calibrate the result.

Training from the base model instead (the recipes in `configs/v1/`) is for a user who wants a
different recipe, not only their data added. It needs the full corpus and teacher files
(`training/README.md`, "The v1 release recipes") and many more GPU hours.

## Environment

- An NVIDIA GPU. Qwen3.5 torsos need Linux (or WSL2) and `flash-linear-attention`; Gemma 4 torsos
  need transformers 5.15 or later. Install with `pip install -e ".[train,dev]"` plus the pinned
  packages of `training/README.md` "Setup".
- `init_from` the released model of the size the user will serve (Phase 4).

## Hosts

Peak GPU memory per rank at micro-batch 8, gradient checkpointing on, 4,096-token window
(`training/README.md`), and a one-GPU host that fits it:

| torso | peak memory | one GPU that fits | notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3.5 2B | under 24 GiB | 24 GB (RTX 3090/4090, L4) or larger | about 11 h for the full v19 recipe on one RTX 3090 |
| Gemma 4 E2B | 14.5 GiB | 24 GB or larger | `host_embeddings: true` saves 4.4 GiB on one GPU |
| Gemma 4 E4B | 19.9 GiB | 48 GB (L40S) is safe; 24 GB is tight | `host_embeddings: true` on one GPU |
| Gemma 4 12B | 28.6 GiB | 48 GB (L40S) or 80 GB (H100) | |
| Gemma 4 26B-A4B | 52.9 GiB | 80 GB (H100) | |

On AWS, `training/aws/scripts/launch-host.sh` defaults to 8-GPU shapes (`SHAPES` in
`training/aws/README.md`). For one GPU, pass a one-GPU shape, for example
`SHAPES="g6e.xlarge"` (one L40S, 48 GB) or a one-H100 shape where the region has one. Look up the
hourly price for the shape and region, give the user the shape, region, hours and price, and wait
for a yes (`training/AGENTS.md` section 0). Eight GPUs train one run about 8 times faster with
`torchrun` (below), at about 8 times the hourly price.

Time: training prints the number of optimizer steps; the smoke run gives the time per step.

## Data to the host

`sync-code.sh` ships one git commit, and the user's data must never be committed. Copy the frozen
`work/` files through a bucket the user owns, after the user agrees that the data may go there:

```bash
# on your machine
aws s3 cp --recursive work/train s3://<user-bucket>/<run>/work/train
aws s3 cp --recursive work/eval  s3://<user-bucket>/<run>/work/eval
aws s3 cp work/train.yaml s3://<user-bucket>/<run>/work/train.yaml
# on the host (through ssm-run.sh), into the code directory
aws s3 cp --recursive s3://<user-bucket>/<run>/work /opt/hobson/code/<code-dir>/work
(cd /opt/hobson/code/<code-dir>/work/train && sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS)
```

The host's IAM role must be able to read that bucket. Copy checkpoints back the same way, and
delete the data from the host and the bucket when the user asks.

## Build the public corpus

The public corpus keeps the general skills of the model and its calibration on unfamiliar input.
Use the `data build` command of `training/steps.md` "1. Build the corpora", with three changes:
`--out work/train/public.jsonl`; no `--holdout` options (they write a second file); and
`--max-examples K` to cap the rows per recipe. The command names 28 recipes, so K = (customer rows)
/ 28 gives about one public row per customer row. Its sources and licences are in
`data/sources.md`; the user decides whether those licences suit their use.

## Config template

Save as `work/train.yaml`. Fields are those of `TrainConfig` in `training/train.py`;
`configs/train.yaml` explains each in its comments (but do not copy its architecture keys).

```yaml
init_from: "StrandsAgents/strands-decider-E4B-gemma4-v1-2610"   # the size the user will serve
train_files: ["work/train/train.jsonl", "work/train/public.jsonl"]
val_fraction: 0.03
val_split_seed: 0          # every seed validates on the same rows
# host_embeddings: true    # Gemma E2B and E4B on ONE GPU only; never under torchrun

# Keep the answers close to the released model's own. Lower the weight (0.1) if the user's
# rows do not move enough on the dev half; raise it if the general-skills set falls.
kl_frozen_weight: 0.3
kl_frozen_reference: "StrandsAgents/strands-decider-E4B-gemma4-v1-2610"
precompute_frozen_kl: true # needs group_by_length
group_by_length: true

epochs: 1
micro_batch_size: 8
grad_accum: 4              # 32 rows per optimizer step
lr: 0.0001
head_lr: 0.0001            # the head is already trained; 1e-3 (the default) is for a new head
weight_decay: 0.01
warmup_ratio: 0.03
max_grad_norm: 1.0
gradient_checkpointing: true
shuffle_options: true      # never turn this off
head_dropout: 0.05
ordinal_smoothing: 0.1
reverse_score_prob: 0.5

seed: 0
output_dir: "work/ckpt/s0"
log_every: 20
eval_every: 500           # set to about steps / 5 after the smoke run
```

No teacher file: the user's rows have gold labels, and a teacher file attaches to rows by
position. The learning rates are starting points, not measured optima for fine-tuning; if the
smoke run's loss does not fall, or the first full seed moves the dev half less than expected,
try `lr` 2e-4 on one seed before you train three.

## Smoke run

```bash
sed -e 's/^log_every: .*/log_every: 2/' work/train.yaml > work/train-smoke.yaml
python -m training.train --config work/train-smoke.yaml --output-dir work/ckpt/smoke --max-steps 20
```

Check the printed lines. Stop at the first one that fails, and do not start the full runs:

- `continuing from <checkpoint>`: training starts from the released model. If the run prints
  only `loading base model â€¦`, it is not fine-tuning the release; check `init_from`.
- `trainable N / M (P%)`: P must be at least 1%. From a released Qwen3.5 2B soup it is 53.6M of
  1.94B (2.77%). Below 1% means the adapter is frozen and only a head trains: stop.
- `train=T val=V`: the row counts you expect.
- A loss line every 2 steps, and a loss that falls over the 20 steps.

Then estimate the full run, and give the user the time and its cost before the full runs:

- Steps: with `--max-steps` the printed step count is 20, so compute
  steps â‰ˆ T / (micro_batch_size Ã— grad_accum) Ã— epochs.
- Training time â‰ˆ steps / the `step/s` printed on the last smoke loss line. Do not use the smoke
  run's wall time / 20: it includes fixed costs that do not grow with the steps.
- Fixed cost per run: the model load, and with `precompute_frozen_kl` the
  `frozen-KL reference for N micro-batches in S s` line. The precompute covers every training
  row, but do not scale the smoke run's line linearly (S Ã— (T / micro_batch_size) / N): the
  smoke run's precompute carries start-up overhead. In the measured example below, linear
  scaling predicted 22 min and the run took 9. Report it to the user as a fixed cost of a few
  minutes to tens of minutes per seed, and add it once per seed.
- Set `eval_every` to about steps / 5 in `work/train.yaml`, so that the `eval @ <step>` lines of
  "Monitoring" appear during the run. With the template's 500, a run under 500 steps prints only
  the final evaluation.

Measured example, 2B soup on one L4: 432 steps at 0.22 to 0.23 step/s, 31 min of training,
plus about 9 min of frozen-KL precompute: 41 min per seed. The smoke run's wall time / 20 would
have predicted 82 min.

## Three seeds

```bash
for s in 0 1 2; do
  sed -e "s/^seed: .*/seed: $s/" -e "s#^output_dir: .*#output_dir: \"work/ckpt/s$s\"#" \
    work/train.yaml > work/train-s$s.yaml
  python -m training.train --config work/train-s$s.yaml
done
# or one run on eight GPUs (without host_embeddings)
torchrun --standalone --nproc_per_node=8 -m training.train --config work/train-s0.yaml
```

On a cloud host, run long jobs in the background as `training/AGENTS.md` describes, not in a
held-open session.

## Monitoring

Training prints a loss line every `log_every` steps (and `kl` when `kl_frozen_weight` > 0), and
`eval @ <step>: {'val_loss': â€¦, 'val_acc': â€¦}` every `eval_every` steps. At the end it writes
`history.json` into `output_dir`. Watch for:

- **Healthy:** the loss falls fast in the first few hundred steps, then slowly; `val_loss` falls
  and `val_acc` rises, then both flatten.
- **Divergence:** the loss rises and stays up, or becomes NaN. Stop the run; do not soup it. Retry
  with half the `lr`, and report it.
- **Overfitting:** `val_loss` rises while the training loss still falls. With one epoch this is
  rare; if it happens, the customer rows are probably repeated too often.
- **Seeds disagree:** compare the three `history.json` files. One seed far from the other two is a
  failed run, not a lucky one.

## Calibration quality

After training, for each seed, score the uncalibrated model:

```bash
python -m training.evaluate eval work/ckpt/s0 --data work/eval/eval.jsonl --limit 1000000 --raw
```

Then soup, calibrate and evaluate (SKILL.md Phase 7). Check:

- ECE on the test half falls after calibration, and stays below the released model's ECE on the
  same half.
- The accuracy at the Phase 8 thresholds meets the user's target for automatic action.
- The `by_confidence_band` table: accuracy should rise with the band. A band whose accuracy is
  below a lower band means the confidence is not usable there.
- `noul` answers near 0.5: many more than the released model means the model hedges; it fails the
  user's automation even when accuracy is the same.

Calibration cannot change a `choice` pick, so choice accuracy does not change. It does change
`noul` and `score` values.

## Soup

`python -m training.soup` averages the three seeds exactly (LoRA updates and head logits) and resets
the temperatures; calibrate it before you evaluate or serve it. The seeds must share one recipe and
one base revision (`training/steps.md` "Seeds and soups").

"""The strands-decider CLI: ask and serve.

Training, evaluation, calibration and corpus-building live outside this package.
Run them as `python -m training.train`, `python -m training.evaluate`,
`python -m training.soup` and `python -m training.data` (see training/README.md).
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import atexit
import logging
import os
import sys

import torch
import typer
from rich.console import Console

from .schema import ChoiceQuestion, NoulQuestion, Question, ScoreQuestion, SystemOneResponse

app = typer.Typer(
    name="strands-decider",
    help="A System One model: typed, calibrated answers instead of text.",
    no_args_is_help=True,
    add_completion=False,
)

console = Console()


def _auto_device() -> str:
    """Best available torch device: cuda > mps > cpu. MLX is opt-in (`--device mlx`)."""
    if torch.cuda.is_available():
        return "cuda"
    if getattr(torch.backends, "mps", None) is not None and torch.backends.mps.is_available():
        return "mps"
    return "cpu"


def _configure_inference_logging(device: str) -> None:
    if str(device).split(":", 1)[0] in {"cpu", "mps", "mlx"}:
        logging.getLogger("transformers.integrations.hub_kernels").setLevel(logging.ERROR)


def resolve_device(device: str | None) -> str:
    """Pick the torch device and silence the hub_kernels noise it would otherwise emit."""
    selected = device or _auto_device()
    _configure_inference_logging(selected)
    return selected


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- serve / ask


@app.command("serve")
def serve_cmd(
    checkpoint: str = typer.Argument(...),
    host: str = typer.Option("127.0.0.1"),
    port: int = typer.Option(8000),
    device: str | None = typer.Option(
        None, "--device",
        help="cuda, mps or cpu (torch), or mlx (Apple silicon, needs the mlx extra). "
        "Auto-detected when omitted: cuda > mps > cpu; mlx only when asked for.",
    ),
    no_prefix_cache: bool = typer.Option(False, "--no-prefix-cache"),
    model_name: str | None = typer.Option(
        None, "--model-name",
        help="Value returned as `model` in responses. Defaults to the checkpoint basename.",
    ),
    strict_window: bool = typer.Option(
        False, "--strict-window",
        help="Reject (HTTP 422) a prompt longer than the context window instead of truncating it.",
    ),
    vision: bool = typer.Option(
        False, "--vision",
        help="Keep Qwen3.5's vision tower so requests may carry `images` (docs/vision.md).",
    ),
    max_batch: int = typer.Option(
        32, "--max-batch", help="Questions encoded per forward pass; lower it for very long states.",
    ),
    max_batch_tokens: int | None = typer.Option(
        None, "--max-batch-tokens",
        help="Also cap one forward's padded tokens (questions x longest state + question); for long-context torsos.",
    ),
) -> None:
    """Serve POST /v1/systemone. JevBench's typesafe adapter runs against it unchanged."""
    from .server import serve

    selected_device = resolve_device(device)
    console.print(f"[green]serving[/] {checkpoint} on http://{host}:{port} ({selected_device})")
    serve(
        checkpoint, host=host, port=port, device=selected_device,
        use_prefix_cache=not no_prefix_cache, model_name=model_name,
        strict_window=strict_window, max_batch=max_batch, vision=vision,
        max_batch_tokens=max_batch_tokens,
    )


@app.command("ask")
def ask_cmd(
    checkpoint: str = typer.Argument(...),
    state: str = typer.Option(..., "--state", "-s", help="The content to evaluate."),
    image: list[str] | None = typer.Option(
        None, "--image", help="Image file, part of the state; repeat. Loads the vision tower."
    ),
    noul: list[str] | None = typer.Option(None, "--noul", help="Yes/no question; repeat."),
    choice: list[str] | None = typer.Option(
        None, "--choice", help="'question?=opt1,opt2,opt3'; repeat."
    ),
    score: list[str] | None = typer.Option(
        None, "--score", help="'question?=low,mid,high' (ascending); repeat."
    ),
    device: str | None = typer.Option(
        None, "--device",
        help="cuda, mps or cpu (torch), or mlx (Apple silicon, needs the mlx extra). "
        "Auto-detected when omitted: cuda > mps > cpu; mlx only when asked for.",
    ),
    as_json: bool = typer.Option(False, "--json", help="Print the raw API response."),
) -> None:
    """Ask one state a set of typed questions from the command line."""
    from .infer import EngineConfig, load_engine

    questions: dict[str, Question] = {}
    for i, q in enumerate(noul or []):
        questions[f"noul_{i}"] = NoulQuestion(instructions=q)
    for i, spec in enumerate(choice or []):
        q, _, opts = spec.partition("=")
        if not opts:
            raise typer.BadParameter(f"--choice needs 'question=opt1,opt2': {spec!r}")
        questions[f"choice_{i}"] = ChoiceQuestion(
            instructions=q, criteria={o.strip(): "" for o in opts.split(",") if o.strip()}
        )
    for i, spec in enumerate(score or []):
        q, _, levels = spec.partition("=")
        if not levels:
            raise typer.BadParameter(f"--score needs 'question=low,high': {spec!r}")
        questions[f"score_{i}"] = ScoreQuestion(
            instructions=q, criteria=[s.strip() for s in levels.split(",") if s.strip()]
        )
    if not questions:
        raise typer.BadParameter("ask at least one --noul / --choice / --score question")

    selected_device = resolve_device(device)
    if image:
        import base64

        from .vision import load_vision_engine

        encoded = []
        for path in image:
            with open(path, "rb") as fh:
                encoded.append(base64.b64encode(fh.read()).decode("ascii"))
        response = load_vision_engine(checkpoint, EngineConfig(device=selected_device)).ask_images(
            state, questions, encoded
        )
    else:
        response = load_engine(checkpoint, device=selected_device).ask(state, questions)

    if as_json:
        console.print_json(response.model_dump_json())
    else:
        _print_answers(response)
    # `ask` is done once its answer is printed; see main().
    global _exit_fast
    _exit_fast = True


def _print_answers(response: SystemOneResponse) -> None:
    for name, ans in response.answers.items():
        if ans.type == "noul":
            console.print(f"[bold]{name}[/] noul = [cyan]{ans.noul:.3f}[/]")
        elif ans.type == "choice":
            console.print(
                f"[bold]{name}[/] -> [cyan]{ans.choice}[/] "
                f"(confidence {ans.confidence:.3f})"
            )
            for opt, p in sorted(ans.probabilities.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1]):
                console.print(f"    {opt:<24} {p:.3f}")
        else:
            console.print(
                f"[bold]{name}[/] score = [cyan]{ans.score:.2f}[/] "
                f"(confidence {ans.confidence:.3f})"
            )
            for lvl, p in ans.probabilities.items():
                console.print(f"    {lvl}: {ans.legend.get(lvl, ''):<40} {p:.3f}")


@app.command("info", hidden=True)
def info_cmd(checkpoint: str = typer.Argument(...)) -> None:
    """Print a checkpoint's configuration."""
    from .modeling import StrandsDeciderConfig, checkpoint_dir, config_path

    cfg = StrandsDeciderConfig.from_json(config_path(checkpoint_dir(checkpoint)))
    console.print_json(cfg.to_json())


# Set by a command whose work is finished once it returns; read by main().
_exit_fast = False


def main() -> None:
    """Console-script entry point: `app()`, then a fast exit after a finished `ask`.

    Interpreter shutdown after `ask` takes about 0.5 s on an M3 Pro: torch, MPS and
    every imported module are finalized. A one-shot `ask` holds nothing that needs
    that (no open files, no child processes), so once its answer is printed it runs
    the atexit handlers, flushes and leaves with os._exit. The handlers take a few ms
    and must run: multiprocessing's unlinks the named semaphore behind tqdm's lock (the
    "Loading weights" bar), and without it the resource tracker warns of a leaked
    semaphore after the prompt is back, wherever the start method is spawn or
    forkserver (macOS). Every other command, and anything that calls `app` directly
    (typer's CliRunner, an embedding program), exits normally.
    """
    try:
        app()
    except SystemExit as e:
        code = e.code
    else:
        code = 0
    if not (_exit_fast and code in (0, None)):
        sys.exit(code)
    atexit._run_exitfuncs()  # noqa: SLF001 -- no public API runs the handlers early
    sys.stdout.flush()
    sys.stderr.flush()
    os._exit(0)


if __name__ == "__main__":  # pragma: no cover
    main()



================================================
FILE: src/strands_decider/cpu_kernels.py
================================================
"""A faster depthwise causal convolution for CPU inference of a Qwen3.5 torso.

Each Gated DeltaNet layer runs a short depthwise causal convolution (kernel width 4,
one filter per channel) over its q/k/v projections. Without the `causal_conv1d` CUDA
package, transformers' `causal_conv1d_fn` falls back to
`F.conv1d(..., groups=channels)`. On CPU, PyTorch runs that grouped convolution as one
`_slow_conv2d_forward` call per channel: 6,144 channels times 18 layers is 110,592 calls
per forward. Profiled on an M3 Pro, that was 2.0 of 2.7 s for a 70-token v19 question.

With width 4, the convolution is four shifted multiply-adds over the whole tensor. That
takes 8 ms for all 18 layers instead of 2,026 ms, and agrees with the reference to within
float rounding (`tests/test_cpu_kernels.py`). Linux x86 torch wheels have oneDNN, whose
grouped conv is not per channel; the multiply-adds still beat it there, by 1.1-4x per
layer (docs/inference.md).

`install()` swaps it in for CPU tensors only, the same way `mps_kernels.install()` does
for the chunk rule. Other devices still reach whatever transformers bound.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Any

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

_installed = False


def causal_conv1d_cpu(
    hidden_states: torch.Tensor,
    weight: torch.Tensor,
    bias: torch.Tensor | None = None,
    activation: str | None = None,
    **kwargs: Any,
) -> torch.Tensor:
    """Same contract as transformers' `causal_conv1d_fn`.

    `hidden_states` is [B, C, L] and `weight` is [C, K]. Output position t is
    sum_k weight[:, k] * x[t - (K - 1) + k], with zeros before the sequence starts.
    The input is rounded to the weight dtype, as in the reference. A bf16 or fp16 weight
    accumulates in fp32 and rounds once, as F.conv1d does; separate half-precision
    multiplies and adds would each round. The activation runs in the weight dtype and the
    result is cast back to the input dtype.
    """
    from transformers.activations import ACT2FN

    seq_len = hidden_states.shape[-1]
    width = weight.shape[-1]
    acc = torch.float32 if weight.dtype in (torch.float16, torch.bfloat16) else weight.dtype
    # Channels last, [B, L, C]: the forward passes a transposed view of a [B, L, C]
    # projection and transposes the result back, so each multiply-add then runs over
    # contiguous rows. On a 3,400-token state that is 2x faster than over [B, C, L].
    x = F.pad(hidden_states.to(weight.dtype).to(acc).transpose(1, 2), (0, 0, width - 1, 0))
    w = weight.t().to(acc)
    out = x[:, width - 1 :] * w[width - 1]
    for k in range(width - 1):
        out.addcmul_(x[:, k : k + seq_len], w[k])
    if bias is not None:
        out += bias.to(acc)
    out = out.transpose(1, 2).to(weight.dtype)
    if activation is not None:
        out = ACT2FN[activation](out)
    return out.to(hidden_states.dtype)


def install() -> bool:
    """Route CPU calls of the Qwen3.5 `causal_conv1d_fn` through the version above.

    Idempotent. Returns True if the module function was wrapped, or False if the
    Qwen3.5 model module (or that function) is not present in this transformers.
    """
    global _installed
    if _installed:
        return True
    try:
        from transformers.models.qwen3_5 import modeling_qwen3_5 as q
    except ImportError:
        return False
    current = getattr(q, "causal_conv1d_fn", None)
    if current is None:
        return False

    def dispatch(hidden_states: torch.Tensor, *args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> torch.Tensor:
        if hidden_states.device.type == "cpu":
            return causal_conv1d_cpu(hidden_states, *args, **kwargs)
        out: torch.Tensor = current(hidden_states, *args, **kwargs)
        return out

    dispatch.__wrapped__ = current  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
    q.causal_conv1d_fn = dispatch
    _installed = True
    return True
